tldr.label: Key takeaways
tldr.lead: "Speech to text in Chrome" covers two different jobs. Dictation types your voice into a text field (Gmail, Google Docs, a form). Transcription turns audio that is already playing (a lecture, a video, a call) into a transcript. No single tool is best at both.
bullets: For dictation into any website, Voice In is the most complete Chrome extension: 50+ languages, and the free plan covers Gmail, Google Docs and WhatsApp.
You may not need an extension at all: Google Docs Voice Typing (Tools > Voice typing), Windows voice typing (Win+H) and macOS Dictation are free and already installed.
For transcribing lectures and videos that play in Chrome, LessonScriptor keeps an editable, exportable transcript. Chrome Live Caption shows captions but keeps nothing.

LessonScriptor does NOT type into other websites' text fields. It is a transcription tool, not a dictation tool. Its free mode can hear your own voice through the mic, but the text lands in its own panel.
For live meetings on Google Meet, Zoom or Teams, Tactiq and Otter are built for that job.

intro: A speech-to-text Chrome extension is a browser add-on that turns spoken words into text, but the phrase covers two jobs that need different tools. **Dictation** (also called voice typing) means you speak and the words are typed into the field your cursor is in: a Gmail reply, a Google Doc, a web form. **Transcription** means audio that is already playing, such as a YouTube video, a Moodle or Canvas lecture, or a Zoom call, is turned into a transcript you can keep. Most people searching for a "chrome voice to text extension" want dictation, and the best picks there are Voice In, Speechnotes and Google Docs Voice Typing, plus the free dictation built into Windows (Win+H) and macOS. If you need to transcribe lectures or videos instead, LessonScriptor, Chrome Live Caption, Tactiq and Otter are the tools to compare. We build LessonScriptor, so we'll be clear about where it fits and where it doesn't: it transcribes what plays in Chrome, and it does not type into other sites.

sections.h2: What is the difference between dictation and transcription in Chrome?
sections.body:
Dictation is voice input: Chrome (or your operating system) listens to your microphone and types what you say at the cursor, wherever that cursor is. The output is a sentence in Gmail, a paragraph in Google Docs, a search in a form. You talk, it types, you move on.

Transcription is audio capture: a tool listens to a source, usually a video, a lecture recording or a call, and builds a separate transcript of everything that was said. The output is a document you read, edit and export later.

The two use different audio paths, which is why they are not interchangeable. A dictation extension like Voice In expects one person speaking close to a microphone and inserts short bursts of text into a page. A transcription tool like LessonScriptor expects a long stretch of audio, often from a professor or a video, and keeps all of it in one place. If you pick the wrong category, the tool will technically "work" and still be useless for what you wanted.

callout.label: Which one do you need?
callout.body:
**You want to speak and see the words appear in Gmail, Google Docs, ChatGPT or a form:** you need dictation. Use Google Docs Voice Typing (inside Docs), Win+H on Windows, macOS Dictation, or Voice In / Speechnotes as Chrome extensions. Dragon if you dictate all day for work.

**You want a transcript of a lecture, a YouTube video or a recorded class:** you need transcription. Use LessonScriptor for an editable, exportable transcript, or Chrome Live Caption if you only need to read captions in the moment.

**You want notes from a live Google Meet, Zoom or Teams meeting:** use Tactiq or Otter, which are built around meetings.

**You want to talk through your own ideas and keep the text as notes, not in another app:** LessonScriptor's free mode can do this, since it listens through the mic, but it writes into its own panel. It will not type into Docs or Gmail for you.

sections.h2: What is the best Chrome dictation extension for typing by voice?
sections.body: Voice In is the best Chrome dictation extension for most people because it types straight into the text field you are already using, across a very wide range of sites. Speechnotes is the best pick if you prefer a clean dictation notepad, and Google Docs Voice Typing is the best free option if you write in Docs anyway.

subsections.h3: Voice In: dictation into almost any website
subsections.body:
Voice In is a Chrome extension (also available for Edge) that lets you dictate into editable text across the web: Gmail, Google Docs, ChatGPT, WhatsApp Web, WordPress, Outlook and Salesforce among them. It supports 50+ languages and has built-in voice commands for punctuation on the free plan. The free plan covers popular sites like Gmail, Google Docs and WhatsApp; **Voice In Plus** ($60/year) adds an Advanced Mode for 1,000+ sites, custom voice commands and multi-tab dictation.

**Best for:** anyone who wants one shortcut that works in every tab, from email to chat to CRM forms.

subsections.h3: Speechnotes: a dictation notepad plus a voice-typing extension
subsections.body:
Speechnotes is a free online dictation notepad (speechnotes.co/dictate) with a companion Chrome extension that lets you dictate into forms and text boxes across the web, including Gmail. The dictation tier is free with ads, and Premium removes the ads for $1.90/month. Speechnotes also sells a separate pay-per-minute file transcription service ($0.10/minute) if you have an audio file to upload, which is a different product from the dictation notepad.

**Best for:** writing longer drafts by voice in a distraction-free page, then copying them where they need to go.

subsections.h3: Google Docs Voice Typing: free, built in, Docs only
subsections.body:
Google Docs Voice Typing is Google's built-in dictation, opened from **Tools > Voice typing** (or Ctrl+Shift+S, Cmd+Shift+S on Mac). It works in recent Chrome, Edge and Safari, recognises 100+ languages, and understands spoken punctuation such as "period", "comma" and "new paragraph". Two limits matter: it only types into Google Docs (and Slides speaker notes via Tools > Dictate speaker notes), and voice commands only work in English. School or work accounts can also have it switched off by an administrator.

**Best for:** students drafting essays or notes in Google Docs who don't want to install anything.

subsections.h3: Dragon Professional: heavy-duty dictation on Windows
subsections.body:
Dragon Professional by Nuance (now part of Microsoft) is desktop dictation software for Windows, sold as a one-time licence, with a browser extension that lets it control text fields in Chrome. It is the most trainable option here, with custom vocabularies and commands, and it is overkill unless you dictate for hours a day, for example in legal, medical or accessibility settings. There is no current Mac desktop version.

**Best for:** professionals and users with motor or RSI needs who dictate all day.

sections.h2: Can you use voice typing in Chrome without an extension?
sections.body: Yes. Windows and macOS both include free dictation that types into any text field, including every website you open in Chrome, so for many people the best "voice to text Chrome extension" is the one they already have.

subsections.body: Windows voice typing opens with **Windows key + H** in any text box, on Windows 10 and Windows 11. It works anywhere you have a cursor, so it covers Gmail, Google Docs, Notion and web forms in Chrome without any extension. It inserts punctuation automatically if you turn that setting on, supports 40+ languages and understands commands like "delete that". The catch: it uses Microsoft's online speech recognition (Azure Speech), so it needs an internet connection.

macOS Dictation is turned on in **System Settings > Keyboard > Dictation**, then started with the Microphone key or the shortcut you choose. Apple's documentation describes it as letting you enter text anywhere you can type, which includes Chrome. It adds punctuation automatically in supported languages, lets you keep typing while dictating on Apple silicon Macs, and stops after 30 seconds of silence.

sections.h2: What is the best speech-to-text Chrome extension for lectures and videos?
sections.body: LessonScriptor is the best speech-to-text Chrome extension for transcribing lectures and videos into notes you keep, because it builds an editable transcript in a side panel from anything that plays audio in Chrome. Chrome Live Caption is the quickest option if you only need to read along, and Tactiq or Otter fit better if your main need is live meetings.

subsections.h3: LessonScriptor: an editable transcript of anything playing in Chrome
subsections.body:
LessonScriptor is a Chrome extension that transcribes lectures, YouTube videos and calls into a side panel while they play. It works on university platforms (Moodle, Canvas, Blackboard, Panopto), YouTube, Coursera and Udemy, embedded players, and Zoom, Google Meet or Teams in the browser, including Zoom recordings.

**Free mode ($0, no account)** uses the browser's built-in speech recognition through your **microphone**. It hears the video through your speakers, so the volume needs to be high (80%+ works best) and it does not work with headphones. No audio is sent to LessonScriptor's servers. Because it listens through the mic, it also picks up your own voice, so you can talk through an idea and keep the text as notes.

**AI mode (pay-as-you-go)** captures the tab's audio directly, so it works with headphones and doesn't need the mic. It uses Whisper-class cloud models that handle accents, jargon and background noise much better. Text arrives in short chunks (every 10 seconds in Normal mode, 30 seconds in the more accurate Optimal mode), not word by word. Packs are one-time: 5h for $5, 15h for $12, 30h for $21 (prices in USD; Stripe shows a local-currency estimate at checkout), with credits that never expire and a 30-minute free trial.

The transcript is a note editor: highlight in five colours, bold, add headers and bullets, delete chatter, add a screenshot of the current slide, then export as .txt or .md or copy to the clipboard. It supports 14 languages.

**What LessonScriptor is not:** a dictation tool. It does not type into Google Docs, Gmail, ChatGPT or any other site's text field. If that is what you need, use Voice In, Speechnotes, Docs Voice Typing or Win+H from the section above.

subsections.h3: Chrome Live Caption: free captions that don't stay
subsections.body: Chrome Live Caption is a captioning feature built into desktop Chrome on Windows, Mac, Linux and ChromeOS, turned on in **Settings > Accessibility > Live Caption** (or chrome://settings/accessibility). It captions any audio playing in Chrome, processes it locally, and supports English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Hindi, Simplified and Traditional Chinese and several more. The limit is that captions are a floating box of a couple of lines that disappear: there is no history to save, edit or export. It is ideal for following a video in a noisy room, not for notes.

subsections.h3: Tactiq: live meeting transcripts without a bot
subsections.body: Tactiq is a Chrome extension that transcribes Google Meet, Zoom and Microsoft Teams calls in real time without adding a bot to the call. The free plan includes 10 transcripts a month, and Pro starts at €6.67/month billed annually. It is built around meetings, so it is a strong pick for group projects and seminars on Meet, and not designed for recorded lecture videos.

subsections.h3: Otter: meeting notes and file uploads
subsections.body: Otter is a transcription app with a Chrome extension, best known for meeting notes with speaker detection and summaries. Its free plan includes a monthly allowance of transcription minutes, and it also lets you upload audio or video files. For a video that is playing in a tab, Otter's own guidance is to play it aloud while Otter listens through the microphone, which is the same speakers-to-mic approach as LessonScriptor's free mode.

sections.h2: Which speech-to-text tool should students use?
sections.body:
Most students need both jobs, in different moments of the week, and the free built-in tools cover more than people expect.

**Writing an essay or a reply by voice:** Google Docs Voice Typing if you write in Docs; Win+H or macOS Dictation for everywhere else; Voice In if you want one extension across Gmail, Docs and your LMS forms.

**Watching a recorded lecture on Moodle, Canvas or Panopto, or a YouTube explainer:** LessonScriptor, so the transcript builds while you watch and you can highlight and structure it before the video ends. Use AI mode if you study with headphones or the lecturer has a strong accent or technical vocabulary.

**Following a video in a noisy library with no plan to keep notes:** Chrome Live Caption.

**Group meetings on Google Meet or Teams:** Tactiq.

For students with ADHD, the split matters even more. Writing while listening divides attention; letting a transcript build itself frees working memory to follow the lecture, while dictation helps get ideas out before they slip away. Many students end up using one tool from each column.

sections.h2: Which Chrome speech-to-text option is the most accurate?
sections.body:
Accuracy depends more on the audio than on the brand. Dictation is accurate because the conditions are ideal: one speaker, close to the mic, speaking clearly and pausing for punctuation. Transcription of a lecture is harder: a lecturer across a room, a recording with echo, technical vocabulary and accents.

For dictation, the built-in engines (Google's in Docs and Chrome, Microsoft's Azure-based voice typing, Apple's Dictation) are all good on clear speech in major languages. Dragon is the most trainable if you have unusual vocabulary.

For transcription, browser speech recognition works well on clear audio through speakers, and drops on accents, jargon and noise. Cloud models of the Whisper class, which LessonScriptor uses in AI mode, are noticeably better in those conditions, at the cost of a short delay while each chunk of audio is processed. If a lecture is in French, German or Spanish with a lot of field-specific terms, that gap is where AI mode earns its price.

questions.question: What is the best speech to text Chrome extension for dictation?
questions.answer: Voice In is the best Chrome extension for dictation into any website: it types into Gmail, Google Docs, ChatGPT and other text fields, supports 50+ languages and has a free plan. Speechnotes is a good free alternative with a dictation notepad, and Google Docs Voice Typing is free if you only write in Docs.

questions.question: Does Chrome have built-in speech to text?
questions.answer: Chrome has two built-in pieces. Live Caption (Settings > Accessibility) captions audio that is playing but does not type for you. Google Docs Voice Typing (Tools > Voice typing) dictates into Google Docs only. For voice typing on every website, use Win+H on Windows, macOS Dictation, or an extension like Voice In.

questions.question: How do I voice type in Gmail or Google Forms in Chrome?
questions.answer: Click in the text field and press Windows key + H on Windows, or start macOS Dictation with the Microphone key or your shortcut. Both type into any field in Chrome. If you want a Chrome-only option, install Voice In or the Speechnotes extension.

questions.question: Can LessonScriptor type into Google Docs or Gmail?
questions.answer: No. LessonScriptor is a transcription tool, not a dictation tool: it writes into its own side panel, not into other websites. Its free mode listens through the microphone, so it can capture your own voice as notes, and you can export or copy the text afterwards. For direct voice typing, use Docs Voice Typing, Win+H, macOS Dictation or Voice In.

questions.question: What is the best Chrome extension to transcribe a lecture or YouTube video?
questions.answer: LessonScriptor transcribes anything playing in Chrome, including Moodle, Canvas, Panopto, YouTube and Zoom recordings, into an editable transcript you can export as .txt or .md. Free mode uses the mic and speakers; AI mode captures tab audio, works with headphones and is more accurate on accents and jargon.

questions.question: Is there a free voice to text Chrome extension?
questions.answer: Yes. Voice In and Speechnotes both have free dictation plans, and Google Docs Voice Typing, Windows voice typing and macOS Dictation are free and built in. For transcription, LessonScriptor's free mode and Chrome Live Caption cost nothing.

questions.question: Does speech to text work with headphones in Chrome?
questions.answer: For dictation, yes: headphones don't matter because the tool listens to your mic. For transcribing a video, mic-based tools such as LessonScriptor's free mode need the audio on your speakers. LessonScriptor's AI mode captures tab audio directly, so it works with headphones.

summary.heading: The short answer: pick the tool by the job
summary.body: For dictation and voice typing into Gmail, Google Docs and forms, use Voice In or Speechnotes as Chrome extensions, or the free voice typing already in Google Docs, Windows (Win+H) and macOS. For transcribing lectures and videos that play in Chrome into notes you keep, use LessonScriptor; for read-only captions, Chrome Live Caption; for live meetings, Tactiq or Otter. LessonScriptor does not type into other websites, so if dictation is what you came for, start with the first group.
